items.title: [Sports Science 101 #12] One Body, Many Ages: Why Exercise Should Change As You Grow
items.body:
> The way your body responds to exercise shifts from childhood to old age, and matching your training to your life stage is what keeps you strong, mobile, and healthy for decades.

## Today's Concept

There is no single "correct" workout that fits a person for their whole life. The same body needs different things at age 8, 18, 45, and 75, because it is doing different jobs at each stage: building, peaking, maintaining, and preserving.

A few ideas explain most of it:

- **Kids are still building the frame.** The long bones of children and teens grow at soft zones called **growth plates**, near the ends of the bones. Because kids are constructing coordination and bone at the same time, the priority is *variety and skill*, not heavy loads. The old fear that lifting weights "stunts" a child's growth is not supported by the research. Under good coaching, resistance training is safe and helpful for youth. The real danger is bad technique or trying to lift maximal weight without supervision.

- **Teens hit a growth spurt, then a strength spurt.** During puberty there is a stretch of fastest growth called **Peak Height Velocity (PHV)** — roughly ages 11–12 in girls and 13–14 in boys. Limbs grow before coordination catches up, which is why teens can suddenly look clumsy. Big gains in muscle and strength tend to arrive *after* that height spurt, especially once hormones ramp up.

- **Adults are managing a peak.** Bone mineral density tops out in the late 20s to early 30s. After about age 30, adults slowly lose muscle if they do nothing — a process called **sarcopenia**. Exercise here is maintenance: keep the aerobic engine and the muscle you already built.

- **Older adults are preserving independence.** After 60, muscle and bone loss speed up, and falls become a serious risk. Strength and balance training is not about looking athletic; it is about carrying groceries, climbing stairs, and getting up off the floor safely.

The headline: youth *builds the bank*, adulthood *protects the balance*, and later life *spends it slowly*.

## In Everyday Life

Picture the Martinez family in Ohio, all under one roof.

Eight-year-old Mateo plays in a Little League that costs about $120 for the season. His parents wonder if they should get him "serious" with a weight program. The better bet is what he is already doing — running, throwing, climbing, switching sports across the year. That variety builds coordination and banks bone density he will keep for life.

His sister Sofia, 14, just shot up four inches and keeps tripping over her own feet in soccer. That is PHV at work, not a lack of talent. Her strength gains are coming — they usually follow the height spurt.

Their mom, 46, pays $60 a month for a gym membership but mostly does the treadmill. Adding two short strength sessions a week is what actually fights the muscle loss that has quietly started. And Grandpa, 74, doesn't need a bodybuilder's routine — a few sit-to-stand reps from a kitchen chair and some balance work meaningfully lower his odds of a fall, one of the most common reasons older Americans lose their independence.

Same house, four bodies, four different exercise "prescriptions."

## 3-Line Summary

1. Exercise is not one-size-fits-all; the goal changes with age — build, peak, maintain, then preserve.
2. Supervised resistance training does not stunt kids' growth; the growth-spurt clumsiness of teens is normal and temporary.
3. Bone and muscle you build young are a "bank" you draw on later, so strength and balance training matters most in older age.

## ✅ Self Quiz

1. **True or False:** Properly supervised resistance training stunts a child's growth by damaging the growth plates.
2. **Peak Height Velocity (PHV)** refers to:
   - A) The maximum sprint speed a teen can reach
   - B) The period of fastest height growth during puberty
   - C) The age when bone density peaks
3. **True or False:** The main reason to prioritize strength and balance training for adults over 65 is to reduce the risk of falls and preserve independence.

## 📚 Today's Terms

- **Growth plate (epiphyseal plate):** A zone of cartilage near the ends of a child's long bones where lengthening happens; it hardens and closes after puberty.
- **Peak Height Velocity (PHV):** The point during puberty when a person grows in height fastest, typically earlier in girls than boys.
- **Sarcopenia:** The age-related loss of muscle mass and strength that begins around age 30 and speeds up in later decades.
- **Bone mineral density:** A measure of how much mineral is packed into bone; it peaks in the late 20s to early 30s and is built partly through weight-bearing activity when young.
- **Physical literacy:** The foundation of movement skills — running, jumping, throwing, balancing — that a child develops through varied, playful activity.

---
*Answers: 1) False — under proper supervision, resistance training is considered safe for youth and does not stunt growth; injuries come from poor technique or unsupervised maximal lifting, not from strength training itself. 2) B — PHV is the phase of fastest height growth in puberty, roughly ages 11–12 in girls and 13–14 in boys, and it often arrives before coordination and strength catch up. 3) True — for older adults, strength and balance work mainly protects against falls and helps preserve everyday independence.*

items.title: [AFA 2025] Five Professors Spent Their Own Money on 85,000 Stock Trades to Find Out What "Free" Trading Really Costs
items.body:
> Researchers placed more than 85,000 identical, simultaneous stock orders at different brokerages and found the same trade can cost you noticeably different amounts depending on which app you use — a finding that earned the Dimensional Fund Advisors Distinguished Paper Prize, presented at the American Finance Association's 2025 annual meeting.

## What They Presented

"Zero commission" has been the headline promise of retail stock trading apps since 2019. But is a free trade actually free? Christopher Schwarz (UC Irvine), Brad Barber (UC Davis), Xing Huang (Washington University in St. Louis), Philippe Jorion (UC Irvine), and Terrance Odean (UC Berkeley) decided to test it the hard way: with real money, in real accounts.

From December 2021 to June 2022, the team opened six accounts at five different brokerages and submitted 85,417 market orders — buying and selling the same stocks, in the same quantities, at the same moments, across the different accounts. Because the orders were identical in every way except which broker handled them, any difference in the prices they got could only come from the brokers and the firms executing their trades. The experiment cost the researchers tens of thousands of dollars of their own trading losses.

The results were striking. The average cost of a "round trip" (buying and then selling a stock) ranged from about 0.07% at the best-performing account to about 0.46% at the worst — a gap of more than six times, even with zero commissions everywhere. On the very first day of the pilot, one account lost $150 while another account making the same trades gained $12.

Where does the gap come from? Most retail orders never reach a stock exchange. They are routed to off-exchange firms called wholesalers, which fill the orders and usually give customers a slightly better price than the official quote — so-called "price improvement." The study found that the same wholesalers systematically gave different amounts of price improvement to different brokers for essentially identical orders. Surprisingly, payment for order flow (PFOF) — the controversial money wholesalers pay brokers for sending them orders, and the usual suspect in this debate — did not explain the differences in execution prices across brokers.

The paper was published in the Journal of Finance, and the title's phrase "actual retail price" — familiar to anyone who has watched the game show The Price Is Right — hints at the point: the true price of a retail trade is not the one on the label.

## Why It Matters

Tens of millions of Americans now trade stocks through commission-free apps, and many pick a broker based on design, features, or marketing — assuming execution is the same everywhere. This study shows it is not. For an active trader, a few hundredths of a percent per trade compounds into real money over hundreds of trades a year.

The paper also reshaped a major policy debate. Regulators, including the SEC, had focused heavily on PFOF as the potential hidden cost of free trading. This evidence suggests the bigger issue is the lack of transparency around execution quality itself: brokers deliver measurably different prices, and nothing on your trade confirmation tells you so. As Schwarz put it, it is hard to think of another consumer financial product where costs differ this much without being disclosed. The authors propose more informative, standardized disclosures so investors can actually compare brokers on the thing that matters — the prices they get.

There is a professional lesson here too: the study's power comes from its design. Rather than analyzing messy historical data, the authors ran a clean field experiment — identical orders, same instant, different brokers — which is why a five-person academic team could produce evidence that moved an industry conversation.

## An Easy Way to Get It

Imagine identical twins walking into the same coffee shop at the same second and ordering the exact same latte — but each one orders through a different delivery app. Both apps advertise "no service fee." Yet one twin is quietly charged $4.93 and the other $5.15, because the coffee shop gives different behind-the-scenes discounts to different apps. Neither receipt shows a fee, so neither twin ever knows. That is essentially what this study documented in stock trading: same stock, same moment, same order — different price, depending on the app.

## In Three Lines

1. Researchers placed 85,000+ identical, simultaneous stock orders at five brokerages and found round-trip trading costs varied from roughly 0.07% to 0.46% across accounts, despite zero commissions.
2. The gap comes from wholesalers giving different price improvement to different brokers — and, contrary to expectations, payment for order flow did not explain the differences.
3. "Free" trading has a real, hidden price that varies by broker, and the authors call for clearer execution-quality disclosure so investors can compare.

## 📚 Today's Terms

- **Market order**: An instruction to buy or sell a stock immediately at the best available price, rather than at a price you specify.
- **Price improvement**: When your order is filled at a slightly better price than the official quoted price — for example, buying just under the posted asking price.
- **Payment for order flow (PFOF)**: Money that wholesalers pay brokerages in exchange for routing customer orders to them; a key reason brokers can charge zero commissions.
- **Wholesaler**: An off-exchange trading firm (such as a large market maker) that executes most retail stock orders instead of a public stock exchange.
- **Round-trip cost**: The total cost of buying a stock and then selling it, used here to measure how much value a trader loses to execution prices alone.

items.title: American Shoppers Turn Cautious: Retail Sales Growth Stalls as Gas Prices and Economic Uncertainty Weigh on Households
items.body:
American consumers spent the first half of 2026 doing what they have done for most of the post-pandemic era: keeping the economy moving. June's retail figures suggest that job is getting harder.

Retail sales growth cooled to its weakest pace since January, according to the latest monthly reading, and the slowdown arrived alongside a familiar pressure point — higher prices at the gas pump. Separately, survey work on household spending intentions found roughly **80% of Americans say they are actively trying to spend less**. Taken together, the two data points sketch a picture that economists have been watching for since spring: a consumer who is not retreating, but is unmistakably more selective.

That distinction matters. Consumer spending accounts for roughly two-thirds of U.S. economic activity, so even a modest change in shopping behavior tends to show up in growth forecasts within a quarter or two.

---

## What the June numbers actually said

The headline is less dramatic than the word "stall" might suggest. Sales did not fall off a cliff; growth simply lost momentum, decelerating to the slowest monthly pace in about five months.

A few caveats are worth holding onto before drawing conclusions:

- **Retail sales are reported in dollars, not units.** When prices rise, the same shopping cart produces a larger sales figure. A soft nominal number therefore implies an even softer picture in real, inflation-adjusted terms.
- **Monthly data is noisy and gets revised.** Initial estimates are routinely adjusted in later releases, sometimes materially. One month rarely establishes a trend.
- **Seasonal timing distorts June.** The calendar placement of summer promotional events and school-related shopping can shift several billion dollars of activity between May and June in any given year.

Analysts generally look past the headline to the "control group" measure, which strips out autos, gasoline, building materials and food services, because it feeds more directly into GDP calculations. When that underlying measure softens at the same time as the headline, the signal carries more weight than a single volatile category swing.

---

## The gasoline problem is a math problem

Rising fuel costs hit household budgets through a mechanism that is simple and unforgiving.

Gasoline is close to a non-discretionary purchase for most working Americans. Commutes do not shorten because prices went up. When the per-gallon cost climbs, the extra dollars come out of the same fixed paycheck that funds everything else — which means spending gets reallocated rather than reduced overall.

The reallocation follows a fairly consistent pattern:

1. **Discretionary goods absorb the hit first.** Apparel, home furnishings, electronics upgrades and hobby purchases get postponed.
2. **Restaurant and leisure spending softens next**, often shifting toward cheaper formats rather than disappearing entirely.
3. **Essentials hold, but trade down.** Grocery volumes stay stable while shoppers move toward store brands, larger pack sizes and promotion-driven buying.

The burden is also uneven. Lower-income households spend a substantially larger share of income on fuel and other essentials, so a given increase at the pump squeezes them far more than it does higher earners. This is one reason aggregate spending totals can look reasonably healthy while a large portion of the population reports feeling stretched.

---

## The "80% trying to spend less" signal

Survey findings that four in five Americans are attempting to cut back deserve careful reading rather than alarm.

Intent and behavior are not the same thing. Stated plans to economize consistently run ahead of measured reductions in actual spending — people tell surveys they will cut back more than they ultimately do. What the number does capture reliably is *sentiment direction*, and that direction has turned defensive.

Where this shows up in practice:

- Increased use of comparison shopping and discount tools before purchase
- Longer deliberation periods on big-ticket items
- Migration toward discount and warehouse retail formats
- Greater sensitivity to promotions and loyalty pricing
- Deferred replacement cycles on durable goods

Retailers watch these behaviors closely, because they compress margins even when total revenue holds up. A shopper who buys the same item on discount rather than at full price registers as flat sales and thinner profit.

---

## Why the second half of 2026 is the real question

Forecasters have flagged several reasons why the recent softness might extend rather than reverse.

**Savings buffers have thinned.** The excess savings accumulated earlier in the decade have largely been drawn down for many households, leaving less cushion to smooth over price shocks.

**Credit is doing more of the work.** When spending is increasingly supported by revolving credit rather than income growth, it becomes more sensitive to interest rates and more vulnerable to a pullback if borrowing costs stay elevated.

**Labor income growth is the swing factor.** Consumer spending ultimately tracks employment and wages more than sentiment. As long as hiring holds up and wage gains keep pace with prices, spending tends to prove more durable than surveys imply. A meaningful weakening in the job market would change that calculus quickly.

**Policy uncertainty raises precaution.** Ambiguity about trade measures, tax treatment and interest rate direction encourages both households and businesses to delay commitments. Delay itself is a form of economic drag.

It is worth stating plainly what the data does *not* show: a spending collapse. Slower growth in a consumer economy running near full employment is a normalization story at least as plausible as a downturn story. Distinguishing between the two typically requires two or three more months of data.

---

## What to watch next

Rather than reacting to any single monthly release, these indicators tend to clarify the direction:

| Indicator | Why it matters |
|---|---|
| Weekly jobless claims | Earliest reliable read on labor market stress |
| Real (inflation-adjusted) retail sales | Strips out price effects from the headline |
| Retail sales control group | Feeds directly into GDP estimates |
| Average retail gasoline prices | Direct pressure on discretionary budgets |
| Credit card balances and delinquency rates | Shows whether spending is income- or credit-funded |
| Retailer earnings guidance | Companies see the shopper before the statistics do |

---

## Practical takeaways for households

None of the above requires a dramatic response, but a cautious environment does reward a few basic habits:

- **Recheck the recurring costs first.** Subscriptions, insurance and service plans are usually where the least painful savings sit — no lifestyle change required.
- **Treat fuel as a budget line, not a rounding error.** Consolidating trips and comparing station prices has a measurable annual effect for high-mileage drivers.
- **Build the buffer before the discretionary cuts.** An emergency fund covering several months of essentials is the single most effective protection against income disruption.
- **Be deliberate about big-ticket timing.** Softer demand often produces better promotional pricing later in the year, particularly on durables and home goods.
- **Watch high-interest balances.** Carrying revolving debt through a period of elevated rates is expensive in a way that compounds quietly.

---

## The bottom line

June's retail data does not describe an American consumer in retreat. It describes one doing arithmetic — absorbing higher fuel costs, weighing purchases longer, and trading down where possible while keeping essential spending intact.

Whether that caution becomes a genuine drag on second-half growth depends far less on sentiment surveys than on whether paychecks keep up. As long as employment holds, spending has historically proved more resilient than the mood suggests. If hiring softens while fuel costs stay elevated, the picture changes — and the coming months of data will settle which of those two paths the economy is on.

---

*This article is general information based on publicly reported economic data and survey findings. Economic statistics are preliminary and subject to revision. Nothing here is financial, investment or tax advice; consult a qualified professional about your own circumstances.*

items.title: America's Housing Market Enters a New Phase: Slow Growth and Normalization Replace the Post-Pandemic Boom
items.body:
The defining story of U.S. housing in 2026 is not a crash. It is the slow, sometimes uncomfortable return to ordinary.

After roughly five years in which home values climbed at a pace few forecasters anticipated, the market has settled into something much quieter. Widely cited industry forecasts now cluster around annual national home-price growth of about **1.2% for 2026** — a figure that would sit below the recent rate of consumer inflation and well beneath the double-digit gains recorded during the peak pandemic years. In practical terms, that means a typical American homeowner may end this year with a house worth slightly more in dollars and slightly less in purchasing power.

Economists have a word for this: normalization. It is less dramatic than a downturn and, for many households, harder to read.

---

## From Boom to Baseline

To understand how unusual the current moment is, it helps to remember how unusual the last one was.

Between 2020 and 2022, a rare combination of forces pushed prices up almost everywhere at once: historically low borrowing costs, a sudden reshuffling of where people could live and work, pandemic-era savings, and a construction pipeline that had never fully recovered from the 2008 crisis. Bidding wars became routine in markets that had never seen them. Sellers grew accustomed to listing high and receiving higher.

That combination has now unwound, piece by piece. Borrowing costs are no longer near record lows. Remote-work migration has largely run its course, with many employers consolidating staff back into established metro areas. The savings cushion has thinned. What remains is a market governed by fundamentals — incomes, rates, supply, and demographics — rather than by momentum.

A roughly 1% national growth rate is not, by historical standards, alarming. For much of the 1990s and mid-2010s, home prices grew at modest single-digit rates. The shock is contextual: an entire cohort of buyers, sellers, and agents entered the market during an anomaly and is now experiencing the baseline for the first time.

---

## The Rate Ceiling

Interest rates remain the single heaviest weight on price growth.

Mortgage rates influence housing through a simple arithmetic that buyers feel immediately: every increment in the rate reduces the loan size a given monthly payment can support. When rates rise, either prices adjust downward or buyers step back. In most markets over the past two years, buyers have stepped back — which is why transaction volumes, more than prices, absorbed the initial impact.

Rates also created a second, less obvious drag known as the **lock-in effect**. Millions of households refinanced or purchased at rates far below what is available today. For those owners, moving means trading a cheap loan for an expensive one, even if the new house costs the same. Many have simply chosen not to move. That decision, repeated across the country, has kept existing homes off the market and suppressed the natural turnover that normally lubricates a housing cycle.

The result is a market that is slow in both directions: fewer listings, fewer sales, and prices that drift rather than swing.

---

## Demographics Quietly Change the Math

Beneath the rate story sits a slower-moving one.

The large millennial cohort that drove first-time buying demand through the late 2010s and early 2020s has now largely passed through its peak household-formation years. The generation behind it is smaller and, on average, entering the market later — delayed by student debt, higher entry prices, and a rental market that has only recently begun to soften in some metros.

At the other end, an aging population is reshaping supply in ways that unfold over decades rather than quarters. Older homeowners are staying in place longer than previous generations did, supported by better health outcomes, accessible home modifications, and a strong preference for aging in place. Housing units that would once have returned to the market through downsizing are instead staying occupied.

Demographers generally expect this to loosen gradually through the 2030s. That is a long horizon for anyone hoping demographic change will relieve today's affordability pressure.

---

## A New Variable: Labor Market Restructuring

The newest factor in the 2026 picture is employment — specifically, the wave of corporate restructuring associated with rapid adoption of artificial intelligence.

The effects so far appear concentrated rather than universal. Reductions have been most visible in white-collar functions that AI tools now partially automate: certain categories of software work, customer support, back-office processing, marketing operations, and portions of business analysis. These are, notably, well-paid roles clustered in expensive metropolitan housing markets.

The housing consequence is less about mass distress than about hesitation. Job security shapes the willingness to take on a thirty-year obligation. When employees in high-income sectors become uncertain about the next two years, some delay purchases, some reduce their price ceiling, and some relocate to lower-cost regions. Aggregate that behavior across a few large metros and it registers as softer demand at the upper-middle tier of the market — precisely the segment that drove much of the previous appreciation.

It is worth being careful here. Economists remain divided about how much of recent labor-market softness is attributable to AI specifically versus broader cost discipline, post-expansion correction, and interest-rate effects working through corporate budgets. The honest position is that AI is one contributor among several, and its full effect will only be measurable in hindsight.

---

## The Inventory Paradox

Everything above describes weaker demand. Ordinarily, weaker demand plus flat supply produces falling prices. That is not what is happening — and inventory explains why.

By most measures, the number of homes available for sale in the United States remains well below pre-2020 norms. The country underbuilt for roughly a decade after the financial crisis, and construction since then has not closed the gap. Homebuilders face elevated financing costs, constrained lots in the most desirable areas, labor shortages in the skilled trades, and local permitting processes that add both time and expense. Meanwhile, the lock-in effect keeps existing inventory frozen.

This produces the defining paradox of the current market: **demand is cooling, but supply is cooling with it.** Prices therefore stall rather than fall. Buyers get relief in the form of time — more days to decide, more room to negotiate, more contingencies accepted — but not, in most places, in the form of meaningfully lower prices.

---

## Regional Divergence Is the Real Story

A national average of 1.2% conceals enormous variation. In practice, 2026 looks like several different housing markets sharing a country.

- **Sun Belt metros that built aggressively** — parts of Texas, Florida, and the Southwest — have added enough new supply that some are seeing flat or modestly declining prices, along with rising concessions from builders. These are the markets where buyers currently hold the most leverage.
- **Coastal and high-cost metros** remain expensive and supply-starved, but face concentrated exposure to white-collar employment shifts. Price growth here is slow, transaction volume is thin, and outcomes vary sharply by neighborhood and price band.
- **Midwest and interior Northeast markets** have generally held up better than expected. Lower entry prices, steadier local employment, and modest speculative activity during the boom left them with less to give back.
- **Insurance-stressed regions** — particularly coastal and wildfire-exposed areas — face a newer pressure: rising premiums that raise the true monthly cost of ownership even when the mortgage does not change.

Anyone reading a national headline should assume it describes their own market only by coincidence.

---

## What It Means in Practice

For **buyers**, conditions are the least frantic in years. Inspection contingencies are back. Negotiation is possible. The trade-off is that affordability is still governed by monthly payment, not sticker price, so the calculation depends heavily on rates and on how long one expects to stay.

For **sellers**, pricing accuracy matters more than at any point in the past five years. Homes priced to the last comparable sale of 2022 tend to sit, and listings that sit tend to sell for less than those priced correctly at the outset.

For **existing owners**, the practical effect of ~1% growth is that housing wealth is no longer compounding quickly. Equity accumulation now comes mainly from paying down principal rather than from appreciation — a return to how home equity historically worked.

For **renters**, softening in some metros reflects the delivery of apartment supply that broke ground during the boom. That pipeline is now thinning, which may limit how long the relief lasts.

---

## What to Watch Through Year-End

Several indicators will show which way the market breaks before national price data catches up:

1. **New listings volume** — a genuine rise would signal the lock-in effect loosening.
2. **Months of supply by metro** — the clearest local measure of buyer versus seller leverage.
3. **Builder incentives and rate buydowns** — an early read on new-construction demand.
4. **White-collar hiring and layoff announcements** in major metros — the leading edge of the labor-market channel.
5. **Insurance and property-tax trends** — increasingly decisive for total ownership cost in exposed regions.

---

## The Takeaway

The post-pandemic housing boom was an exception, not a new normal. What is replacing it is a slower market defined by tension rather than direction: constrained supply pushing up, cautious demand pulling down, and prices caught largely in between.

Normalization is not comfortable for everyone. It is difficult for sellers anchored to 2022 valuations, and it offers less relief to buyers than the phrase "cooling market" suggests. But it is a more sustainable footing than the one that preceded it — and after several years of extraordinary volatility, ordinary may be the more useful thing to plan around.

---

*This article is provided for general information and educational purposes only. It reflects publicly discussed market conditions and forecasts as of mid-2026, which may change. Housing markets vary substantially by region and by individual circumstance. Nothing here constitutes financial, investment, tax, legal, or real estate advice. Readers should consult qualified professionals before making decisions about buying, selling, or financing a home.*
